bc_meadow.blurb: Meadow is a small boulder cluster on the way to Kokanee Lake in the West Kootenay region, inside the Kokanee Glacier park zone near Nelson. It holds eight problems, spread from an easy V2 through a handful of V4s up to a few much harder lines near the top of the scale. The anchor of the zone is a big boulder sitting on the hillside, the first one you meet after leaving the lake trail. Reaching it means a long hike from the Gibson Lake trailhead, down into a meadow and then up through talus, following cairns. Landings are reported as good, and bringing pads is part of the plan.

bc_ladybird_roof.blurb: Ladybird Roof is a steep roof boulder sitting right beside the creek in the Ladybird Creek bouldering zone of the West Kootenays. Eight problems are packed onto it, running from a couple of easy warm-ups at the bottom of the scale through moderate lines around V5 to some serious roof testpieces at V9 and above, so it suits strong boulderers more than beginners. Its position next to the creek makes it one of the quickest stops in the valley: a well-worn trail drops from the main pullout down the bank to the base in well under a minute.
bc_ladybird_roof.approach: A well-used trail leaves almost directly from the main pullout and drops down the bank toward the creek; the boulder is at the bottom, about 30 seconds away.

bc_big_house.blurb: Big House is a sport crag within Rogues Gallery in Cheakamus Canyon, between Squamish and Whistler. It has eight bolted routes, all in the 5.10 to 5.12 range and weighted toward 5.12, so it is a place for people who already lead at that level. There are two main walls. One carries longer lines of roughly 25 to 30 metres; the other has shorter, steeper, bouldery climbs of around 15 metres. Newer development has been added on both flanks. The wider Rogues Gallery has walls close together, which makes it easy to combine several in a day.

bc_sleeping_princess_area_ftgu_centre.blurb: Sleeping Princess Area is the middle section of the From The Ground Up crag, on the lowest tier of Harrison Bluffs in the Fraser Valley. Eight routes are gathered around a pair of parallel cracks, five of them trad and three sport, with grades from 5.7 up to 5.12. Several of the crack lines can also be set up as top-ropes. Getting onto the ledge means a fixed rope or the slab to its right. The crag as a whole is just a minute from the powerline road, giving it the shortest walk of any Harrison Bluffs area, and it can stay damp in early spring.

bc_blackfoot_area.blurb: Blackfoot Area is a roadside ice crag beside the Trans-Canada Highway near Revelstoke, with eight water ice lines. The grades run from WI3 to WI5: three easier routes, two at WI4 and three at WI5, so there is something for newer ice leaders as well as people after steeper climbing. Local conditions reports have listed it among the Revelstoke ice that comes into shape and gets climbed, which makes it one of the more reliable stops in the valley when the cold arrives.

bc_cosmic_lights.blurb: Cosmic Lights is an off-vertical basalt wall of about 15 to 20 metres in the South Cliffs sector of Mt Wells, near Victoria on Vancouver Island. It sits on a big ledge above The Snooze and to the left of The Schoolyard Wall. Eight routes share the face: seven sport lines and one trad line, graded from 5.7 to 5.10, with most of them in the 5.9 to 5.10 band. That mix makes it a friendly place for climbers stepping up from easier grades, and a top-rope can be arranged on one of the lines.

bc_lower_kitselas.blurb: Lower Kitselas is a small wall near Terrace in northern British Columbia, set a few minutes along the trail beyond the main walls of the Kitselas crag. It has eight routes, five trad and three sport, with grades from 5.9 to 5.13 and most clustered around 5.10 and 5.11. The climbing is quite unlike the other Kitselas walls. A walk of about three minutes from the parking area, passing Mail Wall and Lone Route Wall, brings you to a spot where the trail turns left and drops beside a tall bolted face.
